query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing a portion of heavier elements (e.g., Hf or Ta) with a lighter element such as Al in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy can significantly reduce its density while preserving its mechanical properties (strength, hardness) from room temperature to at least 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with density 10.21 g cm−3, known for high strength at room and elevated temperature.
generation.intervention: Partial substitution of approximately 10–20 at% of heavier elements, such as Hf or Ta, with Al in the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr composition during arc-melting synthesis.
generation.conditions: Arc melting under vacuum or inert atmosphere. Homogenization heat treatment at a temperature near 1200–1300 °C, followed by mechanical testing from room temperature to ~1000 °C under comparable loading conditions and strain rates to those used for the baseline alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of Al-containing BCC solid solution, possibly accompanied by minor ordering or precipitation that preserves or enhances mechanical stability at elevated temperatures.
generation.mechanism: The reduced atomic mass and partial formation of supportive BCC or B2-type phases through Al substitution lowers overall alloy density. Higher entropy of mixing and potential microstructural refinements help maintain mechanical strength and hardness from room to elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced density by ~5–10% relative to 10.21 g cm−3, with comparable or slightly improved yield strength at room temperature and ~1000 °C.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a 10.21 g cm−3 density, demonstrating high strength at both ambient and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The substitution level of Al should remain moderate (<25 at%) to prevent excessive formation of brittle or deleterious phases and ensure good mechanical properties are retained.
generation.uncertainty: Exact fraction of Al needed to maximize density reduction yet maintain mechanical properties remains unclear; mechanical and microstructural data for high Al content at temperatures above ~1000 °C are limited.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce and characterize a series of HfMoTaTiZr-based alloys with increasing Al content (0–20 at%) substituted for Hf or Ta via vacuum arc melting, followed by homogenization (~1200 °C). Measure density (Archimedes method) and perform hardness, tensile or compression tests at room temperature, 800 °C, and 1000 °C.
measurements: Yield strength and fracture elongation at room temperature, 800 °C, and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If density is not significantly reduced (>5%), or if strength or ductility at room or elevated temperature declines by more than ~10% compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: According to the traditional alloy design theory, ordered phases or intermetallic compounds will form as the number of alloying elements increases. However, Yeh et al. observes that simple solid solution phases, instead of intermetallic compounds, are formed in an equiatomic quinary alloy. Subsequently, they propose a new alloy system, termed high entropy alloys (HEAs), which contain at least five principal elements, each having the atomic percentage between 5% and 35% [ [1] , [2] ]. Since the development of HEAs, a substantial number of studies on HEA have been performed. Some of these studies are focused on alloys comprised of elements with low melting points, such as AlCoCrCuFeNi system alloys [ [3] , [4] ], commonly exhibiting high ductility and low strength. On the other hand, refractory HEAs have exhibited advantages of high yield strength at room and elevated temperature. For example, Nb25Mo25Ta25W25 and V20Nb20Mo20Ta20 refractory HEAs produced by vacuum arc-melting exhibit compressive yield strengths of 1058 MPa and 1246 MPa, respectively, with plasticities of less than 2% at room temperature [ [5] ]. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. chosen.why: Substituting heavier elements with Al or another light metal lowers density while preserving or improving mechanical properties in refractory high-entropy alloys. Prior studies confirm that Al additions can stabilize BCC phases and maintain high-temperature strength. We hypothesize that density will decrease alongside maintained mechanical performance from RT to ~1000 °C. The hypothesis is tested by producing such modified alloys via arc melting, measuring density and mechanical properties (hardness, yield strength, etc.) at elevated temperatures. The hypothesis is rejected if these modified alloys do not show reduced density or if strength at either RT or 1000 °C falls significantly below that of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr reference alloy.
